summary.title: Spectro-temporal study of atoll source GX 9+9 observed with AstroSat
summary.authors: Sree Bhattacherjee, Arbind Pradhan, Biplob Sarkar
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a comprehensive spectro-temporal analysis of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) GX 9+9, an established atoll source, utilizing data from India's AstroSat mission. The observation, conducted on July 25, 2020, captured the source in the soft/banana state (BS), characterized by a disk-dominated energy spectrum ranging from 0.7 to 25.0 keV. The researchers employed simultaneous data from the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) and the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) to perform flux-resolved spectral analysis across three distinct flux levels. Spectral modeling revealed a best-fit model of const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), yielding an average inner-disk radius of approximately 16.57 km and total unabsorbed fluxes increasing with flux level. Temporal analysis of the LAXPC data identified broad-band noise (BBN) features centered around 0.1 Hz, with no quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) detected. By applying a radiative propagation model formalized by Garg et al., the study determined that the observed variability originates from variations in the inner-disk temperature and the fractional scattering of seed photons in the corona, with a measurable phase lag indicating the propagation of perturbations from the disk to the corona. The findings provide new constraints on the physical parameters of GX 9+9 and offer insights into the radiative mechanisms driving variability in atoll sources.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a comprehensive spectro-temporal analysis of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) GX 9+9, an established atoll source, utilizing data from India's AstroSat mission. The observation, conducted on July 25, 2020, captured the source in the soft/banana state (BS), characterized by a disk-dominated energy spectrum ranging from 0.7 to 25.0 keV. The researchers employed simultaneous data from the Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) and the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) to perform flux-resolved spectral analysis across three distinct flux levels. Spectral modeling revealed a best-fit model of const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), yielding an average inner-disk radius of approximately 16.57 km and total unabsorbed fluxes increasing with flux level. Temporal analysis of the LAXPC data identified broad-band noise (BBN) features centered around 0.1 Hz, with no quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) detected. By applying a radiative propagation model formalized by Garg et al., the study determined that the observed variability originates from variations in the inner-disk temperature and the fractional scattering of seed photons in the corona, with a measurable phase lag indicating the propagation of perturbations from the disk to the corona. The findings provide new constraints on the physical parameters of GX 9+9 and offer insights into the radiative mechanisms driving variability in atoll sources.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary identified during a sounding rocket mission. Atoll sources trace a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram and exhibit two primary states. The hard state is dominated by Comptonization, while the soft state is dominated by accretion disk thermal emission. GX 9+9 shows 4.2-hour modulation and is often detected in a luminous soft state with ~220 mCrab flux. Previous spectral modeling has utilized power laws, blackbodies, and Comptonization models with geometric ambiguities. Recent studies have emphasized the role of spectral modeling in understanding coronal plasma.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. The researchers hypothesize that the source was in the soft/banana state during the observation. The study seeks to estimate source characteristics like inner-disk radius, flux, and temperature. It is hypothesized that spectral and temporal analyses can be compared for constancy. The study investigates whether variability originates from the disk or the corona via radiative propagation. The hypothesis is that variations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering drive the observed BBN.

Methodological Details
The study utilized a single archival observation of GX 9+9 taken on July 25, 2020. Data was collected using the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT). LAXPC counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains, so only LAXPC 20 data was used. LAXPC operates over a wide energy band from 3-80 keV. SXT data was processed using the AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b pipeline to generate cleaned level-2 event files. An annular zone with an outer radius of 13 arcmin and an inner radius of 2 arcmin was used for SXT analysis. SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold, necessitating the use of an annular zone. A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty estimation. Spectral analysis was performed using XSPEC (version 12.13.0c) within the HEASOFT (6.31.1) package. The energy range for spectral analysis was 0.7–25.0 keV. Flux levels were segregated into FL1 (450-570 counts/s), FL2 (570-650 counts/s), and FL3 (650-770 counts/s). Timing analysis focused on the LAXPC data due to its high timing resolution in the order of microseconds. Power density spectra (PDS) were generated in a frequency range of 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz. The inner-disk radius was calculated using a relation involving the color-correction factor k=1.7 and inclination angle θ=60 degrees. The source distance was assumed to be 10 kpc for radius calculations.

Procedures And Architectures
The best-fit spectral model was determined to be const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb). The thermal Comptonization model (ThComp) was used as an improved version of nThComp. The energy range was extended with 1000 log bins for the ThComp convolution model. The optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain other parameters during fitting. Instrumental edge models were required at an energy of 2.4 keV to obtain a better fit. Timing analysis utilized the multi-lorentzian approach to the Power Density Spectrum (PDS). Two Lorentzians were required to fit the PDS to describe the broad-band noise feature. The characteristic frequency νc was calculated using the relation νc= √(νo2+HWHM). The radiative origin of variability was modeled using the formalism presented by Garg et al. [29]. The Garg et al. model assumes a truncated disk and a hot electron plasma (corona) in between the inner radius and ISCO. The model relates spectral parameters with physical parameters to understand stochastic variability. The best-fit temporal model involved varying inner-disk temperature (kTin) and fractional scattering (fs) with a time delay. The phase lag was calculated using the relation time lag = phase lag/2πf.

Key Results
The source was identified as being in the soft/banana state based on the Hardness-Intensity Diagram. The total unabsorbed flux in FL1 was estimated to be ~5.94×10-9 ergs s-1 cm-2. The total unabsorbed flux in FL2 was estimated to be ~6.51×10-9 ergs s-1 cm-2. The total unabsorbed flux in FL3 was estimated to be ~7.30×10-9 ergs s-1 cm-2. The average inner-disk radius (Rin) was estimated to be ~16.57±1.29 km. No quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) or prominent broad-band noise (BBN) features were detected initially. A BBN-like feature was observed in a wide centered region in the PDS. Two Lorentzians were required to fit the PDS to model the variability. The centroid frequency (νo) of the Lorentzian fit was obtained to be ~0.04 Hz. The characteristic frequency (νc) was calculated to be ~0.1 Hz. The half width of the spectral feature at half its maximum height (HWHM) was approximately 0.09 Hz. The reduced χ2 value for the Garg et al. model was ~0.80. The best-fit inner-disk temperature (kTin) for FL1 was 1.87±0.03 keV. The best-fit inner-disk temperature (kTin) for FL2 was 2.02±0.06 keV. The best-fit inner-disk temperature (kTin) for FL3 was 2.04±0.12 keV. The best-fit fractional scattering (fs) for FL1 was 0.14±0.02. The best-fit fractional scattering (fs) for FL2 was 0.17±0.04. The best-fit fractional scattering (fs) for FL3 was 0.34±0.10. The phase lag was found to be 0.11±0.08. The variation in kTin was 0.56±0.10%. The variation in fs was 81±32%. The maximum flux reached 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻², comparable to 7.8 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² reported previously. The average estimated Rin is around 16.54±1.78 km, consistent with previous estimates. The study suggests the source is transitioning towards a softer state. The decrease in kTe and increase in Tin indicate the transition to a softer state. Fractional scattering and changes in inner-disk temperature are the causes of the obtained broad-band noise variability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The source is transitioning towards a softer state as indicated by spectral parameter variations. The decrease in kTe and increase in Tin across flux levels indicate the softening of the spectrum. The observed variability is attributed to variations in the inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. The positive phase lag indicates that the perturbation moves from the disk to the corona. The model successfully explains the energy-dependent temporal properties of the source. The study provides new constraints on the physical parameters of GX 9+9. The findings contribute to understanding the radiative mechanisms driving variability in atoll sources.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is constrained due to poor data quality of the source. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, limiting the comparison with previous results. The error bars on the phase lag are consistent within data points, making reliance on phase lag difficult. Further research and various mission observations are necessary for a better understanding. The distance to the source is assumed to be 10 kpc, which may introduce uncertainty. The inclination angle is considered as 60 degrees, which is an assumption.

Claims
The source GX 9+9 was in the soft/banana state during the AstroSat observation. We may infer that the source was in BS at the time of observation based on the form of HID.  
The total unabsorbed flux increases with increasing flux levels (FL1 to FL3). The maximum flux reached 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻².  
The observed broad-band noise variability originates from variations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering. we find that fractional scattering and the change in inner-disk temperature are the causes of the obtained broad-band noise variability.  

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the Hardness-Intensity Diagram (HID) of the source using AstroSat data. Figure 2 shows the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 in the energy range 0.7-25 keV. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit and (right) shows the energy-dependent temporal modeling. Table 1 displays the best-fit parameters for each flux level and the energy-dependent temporal modeling.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the spectro-temporal analysis of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of BBN variability and its radiative origin. 3. The future path involves further research and various mission observations.
